abstract: These notes give a detailed treatment of binary search trees (BSTs), defined as binary trees where each node's key exceeds all keys in its left subtree and is less than all keys in its right subtree. Insertion and lookup both descend from the root by comparing keys, with insertion attaching a new leaf at the empty position reached. Deletion is identified as the most difficult operation, particularly when the node has two children, and the standard remedy is to replace it with its in-order successor. The notes also observe that worst-case performance degrades to O(n) when the tree becomes unbalanced, which motivates self-balancing variants such as AVL and red-black trees.

key_points: A BST requires every node's key to be greater than all keys in its left subtree and less than all keys in its right subtree.
Insertion descends from the root comparing keys and attaches a new leaf at the appropriate empty slot.
Lookup works symmetrically to insertion, descending from the root by key comparisons.
Deletion is the trickiest operation, especially when the deleted node has two children.
For a node with two children, the standard fix is to replace it with its in-order successor.
Worst-case performance degrades to O(n) when the tree becomes unbalanced.
This degradation motivates self-balancing variants such as AVL and red-black trees.
